problem: Every control covered so far in this layer — firewall, IDS/IPS, EDR, SIEM, SOAR — is fundamentally reactive: something has to trigger a rule, match a signature, or cross a threshold before any of them act.

But by definition, a sufficiently careful or novel attacker can operate below those thresholds, avoiding known signatures and staying quiet enough that nothing fires. Real-world compromises are sometimes discovered only months after the initial breach, precisely because nothing in the automated detection stack ever triggered. Threat Hunting exists to answer: what's already happening in our environment that none of our automated tools have caught yet?
concept: Threat Hunting is the proactive, human-led practice of searching through an environment for signs of compromise that automated detection hasn't already flagged — starting from a hypothesis (often informed by threat intelligence, Session 94) rather than waiting for an alert, and using tools like SIEM search (Session 92) and EDR historical queries (Session 91) to test that hypothesis against real data. It inverts the normal detection workflow: instead of 'wait for an alert, then investigate,' it's 'form a theory about what might be happening, then go look for evidence.'

This is the direct answer to the honest limitation named at the end of Session 94: threat intelligence describes known threats, but genuinely novel techniques haven't been reported by anyone yet. Hunting is how a defender looks for the unknown-unknowns rather than only the known-knowns.
deep: Core mechanics and structure of a disciplined threat-hunting practice:

Hypothesis-driven approach — a hunt starts with a specific, testable theory: 'if a threat actor were using technique X, what evidence would that leave in our logs?' rather than an open-ended, unfocused search through all available data.

Intelligence-led hunting — hypotheses frequently originate directly from threat intelligence (Session 94): a new TTP reported for the sector becomes the starting question for a hunt checking whether that specific technique shows up anywhere internally.

Baseline-driven hunting — alternatively, a hunt can start from 'what does normal look like in this specific part of our environment, and what doesn't fit that pattern,' which is the anomaly-detection logic from IDS (Session 89) applied manually and more thoroughly than an automated rule can.

Iterative querying — hunters use SIEM search (Session 92) and EDR historical queries (Session 91) to progressively narrow down evidence, refining the search as each result either supports or rules out the working hypothesis.

Outcome feedback loop — a successful hunt that finds something real should result in a new detection rule (in the SIEM or EDR) so that pattern is caught automatically next time, meaning mature hunting programs continuously convert hunting findings back into automated coverage.
workflow: A simplified hunt cycle, tying directly into the tools from the last several sessions:

1. A hunter forms a hypothesis — perhaps triggered by a new TTP from a threat intelligence feed (Session 94) describing a technique for maintaining persistence on compromised endpoints that wouldn't necessarily trip existing EDR signatures.
2. The hunter queries EDR's historical telemetry (Session 91) across the endpoint fleet, looking for the specific process or file-system pattern associated with that technique.
3. In parallel, the hunter searches SIEM (Session 92) for any correlating network or identity activity that might support or contradict the hypothesis.

4. If evidence supporting the hypothesis is found, it escalates into a formal investigation, potentially triggering Incident Response (Session 100); if nothing is found, the hypothesis is documented as tested-and-cleared, which still has value — it confirms current visibility and coverage against that specific technique.

5. Regardless of outcome, if a genuine gap in automated detection was identified during the hunt, a new SIEM correlation rule or EDR detection logic is created to close that gap going forward — this is what separates disciplined hunting programs from one-off investigation.
enterprise: Threat Hunting is a practice and a skill set layered on top of existing tooling rather than a separate product category — it's the human expertise that gets the most value out of the SIEM and EDR investments already covered in this layer. For an organization the size of FundedNext, formal, scheduled hunting is more likely to exist as a periodic activity performed by a security analyst or team using existing SIEM/EDR tooling, rather than a dedicated always-on function, which is realistic for most mid-size organizations outside of large enterprises with dedicated hunt teams.
dependencies: Threat hunting cannot happen in a vacuum — it depends entirely on:

Rich, queryable data sources already covered — SIEM (Session 92) for correlated search across sources, EDR (Session 91) for endpoint-level historical detail — since a hunter can only find what the underlying data actually captured.
Threat Intelligence (Session 94) — many, though not all, productive hunts start from an intelligence-informed hypothesis rather than a purely open-ended search.

Deep familiarity with what 'normal' looks like in the specific environment — a hunter has to recognize a deviation, which requires genuinely understanding the baseline, echoing the same baseline-dependency IDS anomaly detection has (Session 89), but applied through human judgment rather than an automated rule.

Sufficient log retention — a hunt looking for evidence of a months-old, slow-moving compromise needs historical data to actually go back that far, which ties directly to the retention decisions made in centralized logging (Session 82) and SIEM storage (Session 92).
dependents: New detection rules for SIEM (Session 92) and EDR (Session 91) — the feedback loop described above, converting one-off findings into ongoing automated coverage.
Incident Response (Session 100) — a hunt that finds genuine evidence of compromise transitions directly into a formal incident response process.

MITRE ATT&CK Mapping (Session 103) — hunts are frequently organized and documented against specific ATT&CK techniques, both to structure the hypothesis and to track which techniques the organization has actively hunted for versus never checked.
security: Threat hunting adds real value but comes with its own honest constraints:

It's resource-intensive and skill-dependent — unlike an automated rule that runs continuously for free once built, hunting requires a skilled analyst's time, which makes it inherently limited in scope and frequency compared to automated detection.

A hunt that finds nothing doesn't prove an environment is clean — it only confirms that specific hypothesis wasn't supported by available evidence within the scope searched, not the absence of all possible compromise.

Hunting quality depends heavily on hunter skill and creativity — a formulaic, uninspired hunting program that only ever tests the most obvious hypotheses provides much less real value than one drawing on genuine expertise and current threat intelligence.
Without the feedback loop back into automated detection, hunting value is one-time rather than cumulative — a real risk if findings aren't systematically converted into new rules.
troubleshooting: Threat-hunting-adjacent patterns worth recognizing, even outside a dedicated hunt team:

A hunt query returns overwhelming, unfiltered results — usually indicates the hypothesis was too broad or the query wasn't scoped tightly enough; narrowing the hypothesis before re-querying is more productive than manually sifting a huge result set.

Historical data needed for a hunt isn't available far enough back — a retention/logging gap (Session 82) rather than a hunting-technique problem; worth flagging as a coverage gap in its own right, separate from whatever the original hunt was investigating.

A hunt repeatedly finds the same benign explanation for what looked like a promising lead — worth documenting as a known baseline pattern so future hunts (and analysts) don't re-investigate the same false lead from scratch.
example: Building on the Session 94 phishing-campaign example: suppose the threat intelligence about trading- platform-support impersonation phishing also mentioned that, in other observed incidents, successful phishing led to attackers using legitimate remote-access tools already present on compromised machines to maintain access quietly, specifically to avoid triggering malware-signature-based detection. A hunter, informed by that intelligence, could proactively query EDR telemetry across the CEx floor's endpoint fleet for unusual usage patterns of those same legitimate remote-access tools — unusual timing, unusual destination, unusual frequency — well before any automated alert would have reason to fire, since nothing about legitimate tool usage inherently looks malicious to a signature-based system.

This is an illustrative extension of the Session 94 example showing how a hunting hypothesis would typically be derived and tested, not a description of any actual campaign, hunt, or FundedNext's specific security operations, which I have no visibility into.
cloud: Cloud environments extend threat hunting to cloud-native log sources — cloud audit logs, IAM activity history, cloud-native EDR-equivalent telemetry — with the same hypothesis-driven methodology applied against cloud-specific TTPs (unusual IAM role assumption patterns, for instance, rather than traditional endpoint process trees). The skill and mindset transfer directly; what changes is the specific data sources and the cloud-specific attack techniques a hunter needs to understand to form good hypotheses in that environment.
automation: While hunting itself is fundamentally a human-judgment activity, the repetitive parts of the process — running the same query pattern across an ever-growing dataset, checking new endpoints as they're onboarded — can be scripted and scheduled, freeing analyst time for the genuinely creative hypothesis- generation work. This connects directly back to the SOAR discussion (Session 93): once a hunting technique is validated and well-understood, it's a strong candidate to become an automated SOAR playbook step or a standing SIEM correlation rule, converting one-time hunting effort into ongoing, free detection coverage.
career: Threat hunting is generally considered a more senior, specialized skill within security operations, typically built on top of solid SIEM and EDR experience rather than an entry-level starting point. For your trajectory, it's worth knowing about now as a career direction to grow into over time — the analytical and hypothesis-driven thinking it requires is a natural extension of the same investigative mindset useful in support and troubleshooting work generally, which is a genuine transferable strength from your current CEx experience.

misconceptions: "Threat hunting is just reviewing SIEM alerts more carefully." — Alert review is reactive by definition; hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven, actively searching for things that never generated an alert at all.
"A clean hunt means the environment is definitely secure." — It only means that specific, scoped hypothesis wasn't supported by available evidence — not a guarantee of no compromise anywhere.
"Threat hunting requires no prior tooling investment." — It depends entirely on the data SIEM and EDR already capture; hunting can't find what wasn't logged in the first place.
"Hunting is only for large enterprises with dedicated teams." — Even periodic, informal hunting by an existing security analyst using existing SIEM/EDR tools adds real value at smaller scale.
anchors: Automated detection waits for a trigger; hunting goes looking without one.
Hypothesis first, query second — undirected searching isn't hunting, it's browsing.
A clean hunt confirms coverage for one hypothesis, not overall security.
Good hunting programs close the loop: findings become new automated detection rules.
connections: Threat Hunting is the human, proactive counterpart to everything automated in Sessions 88–93, and it's the direct practical answer to Threat Intelligence's (Session 94) honest limitation — intelligence describes known threats, hunting looks for what hasn't been reported yet. It depends on SIEM search (Session 92) and EDR historical telemetry (Session 91) as its primary tools, and its findings feed forward into new detection rules, Incident Response (Session 100), and MITRE ATT&CK Mapping (Session 103), closing the loop across nearly this entire security layer.
diagram: Reactive detection vs. proactive hunting (text sketch):

Reactive (Sessions 88-93): [Event occurs] --> [Rule/signature matches] --> [Alert fires] --> [Analyst investigates] Proactive (Hunting): [Hypothesis formed] --> [Analyst queries data] --> [Evidence found or not] --> [New rule created either way] The hunting feedback loop (text sketch):
[Threat Intel: new TTP] --> [Hypothesis] --> [Query SIEM/EDR] --> [Finding confirmed] --> [New detection rule built] --> [Automated coverage going forward, no longer needs manual hunting]
lab: A hands-on exercise applying hypothesis-driven thinking to your own machine, extending the EDR lab from Session 91:

6. Form a specific, testable hypothesis about your own machine — for example: 'no legitimate process on this machine should be spawning a command-line interpreter as a child process during normal browsing activity.'

7. Test it: use Get-Process to review currently running processes, and if comfortable, explore Get- WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational' (if Sysmon is installed) or Security log process-creation events (Event ID 4688, if enabled) to look for parent-child process relationships that would violate your hypothesis.

8. Document the outcome the way a real hunt would: hypothesis tested, data source queried, evidence found or not, and — regardless of outcome — what this exercise told you about your own baseline understanding of what 'normal' looks like on your machine.
9. Write one sentence describing what a standing detection rule based on this hypothesis would look like, connecting this lab directly back to the feedback-loop concept from Section 4.
